title: Quantum Advantage with Adaptive Shallow Circuits
authors: Yusen Wu, Yukun Zhang, XIaoming Zhang, Chuan Wang, Xiao Yuan
abstract: Quantum advantage is widely expected to require sufficiently deep circuits, where correlations and global computational structure can grow beyond the reach of efficient classical simulation. This expectation is especially stark for constant-depth circuits with local readout: the expectation value of any fixed local observable lies within a bounded backward lightcone and is therefore classically tractable. Here we show that measurement feedback changes this picture. We establish a strict hierarchy of computational power: at fixed coherent depth, increasing the number of feedback outcomes strictly enlarges the class of functions accessible through a local expectation value. The two ends of this hierarchy exhibit distinct computational regimes. With logarithmic feedback, local expectation values for product-state inputs are efficiently classically simulable. Polynomial feedback, by contrast, enables an explicit family of adaptive shallow circuits to encode prime-field discrete logarithm problem~(DLP) into a fixed single-qubit expectation. Assuming the standard worst-case classical hardness of DLP, estimating this expectation value is classically hard. These results reveal a feedback-driven complexity transition, with further implications for resource lower bounds on DLP and the complexity of local-observable estimation under area-law entanglement. Our results open a new route to quantum advantage with shallow quantum circuits.
summary: This work analyzes quantum computation using shallow circuits that incorporate mid-circuit measurements and classical feedforward. It proves a strict hierarchy of computational power based on the amount of classical information fed back into the circuit. Crucially, it demonstrates that polynomial feedback allows these local measurements to solve classically hard problems like DLP, opening a new pathway for achieving quantum advantage with resource-efficient circuits.
main_problem: The research addresses determining the minimal resource requirements for achieving quantum advantage when measurements are restricted to local observables rather than full state sampling.
main_result: Increasing the amount of classical feedback in adaptive shallow circuits strictly increases computational power, enabling the encoding of classically hard problems like DLP into a single local expectation value with polynomial feedback.
method: The authors establish computational hierarchies by analyzing the class of functions accessible via local expectation values ($\langle O angle$) based on the complexity of the classical feedforward mechanism ($m$).
model_or_system: The model is Adaptive Shallow Circuits (CRAS) featuring constant coherent depth layers interleaved with mid-circuit measurements and classical feedforward, culminating in a single fixed local observable measurement.
key_observables: Local expectation value ($\langle O angle$) of a fixed single-qubit observable; the required amount of classical feedback ($m$).
important_parameters: The scaling of classical feedback $m$ (e.g., $O(\log n)$ vs. polynomial in $n$); computational depth ($d$).
main_assumptions: The hardness results are conditional on the standard worst-case classical hardness of the Discrete Logarithm Problem (DLP).
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the transition from non-adaptive to adaptive circuits, showing how feedback enables global processing. Other figures detail the construction of complex gates like controlled rotations and Threshold gates on a 2D lattice.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the computational hierarchy using DLP hardness for local readout (Chunk 1 & 2). It then provides detailed constructions demonstrating that complex logical operations, including arithmetic circuits, can be implemented efficiently in terms of depth and rounds on a 2D nearest-neighbor architecture (Chunk 3 & 4).
why_interesting: It provides concrete, resource-aware benchmarks for quantum advantage by showing how adaptive measurement feedback fundamentally changes the complexity landscape compared to static entanglement measures.

FIG. 3. Threshold gate count and depth estimation: We evaluated the threshold-gate count (depth) for 10 ≤n ≤120. A least-squares fit of the gate count indicates an approximately O(n3) scaling. Moreover, assuming sufficiently many ancilla qubits, the threshold gates in each stage can be evaluated in parallel, so the resulting circuit depth remains constant.
